rows.evidence: Q1: Materials and Methods / Table 4 - two-year field experiment (2012-2013) in Inner Mongolia with five drip fertigation levels in a randomized block design, reporting own yield, IWP and PFP data.
rows.notes: The study's treatment variable is fertilizer rate (10-110% of recommended NPK), all plots under the same SMP-based drip irrigation. There is no comparison of drip against another irrigation method, and no measurement of evaporation, runoff, deep percolation or water savings. It reports total irrigation amounts (92.6-173.2 mm) and irrigation water productivity under drip, and compares yields (not water use) with local LEPA enterprises. Hence it provides no own result on drip irrigation conserving water by minimizing evaporation and runoff; analogous to a fertigation-level trial under drip being evidence about fertilizer rate, not about drip.

rows.evidence: Q1: Materials and Methods / Table 4 - two-year field experiment on sand/loamy sand soils with five drip fertigation levels, reporting own yield, IWP and PFP results.
rows.notes: The study was conducted on sandy soil under drip, but it does not test drip against traditional irrigation methods and does not measure water wastage, runoff, percolation or evaporation. All treatments received drip irrigation scheduled at -25 kPa SMP; only fertilizer rate varied. It reports that SMP at 20 cm was kept above -25 kPa for most of the season (Figs 2-3) and gives irrigation amounts and IWP by fertigation level (Table 4), but no own evidence that drip reduces water wastage relative to other methods in sandy soils. The claimed effect is asserted in the introduction (citing other work), not shown by the study's results.

notes: Full text appears complete. Primary two-year field trial on potato fertigation levels under drip on sandy soil; it provides no comparative evidence on drip irrigation's water-conservation effect, which is the subject of both claim rows.
